blocks.text: A grant writer's Mac holds a lot at once. There is the funder's notice in a PDF, the Grants.gov workspace in a browser, a Word draft, a budget spreadsheet, and a few email threads with program staff. Lazur works across all of that. It sees the screen while you hold the shortcut, points at things, and explains what it sees. It does not operate other apps for you.
Where a grant writer's day goes

Instrumentl's grant writer guide splits the working day into four parts. Mornings go to research and preparation. Midday goes to drafting. The afternoon goes to managing and talking with internal and external contacts. The day ends with deadlines and prospect research. The guide gives no time figures, so treat that split as a shape, not a measurement.

No study found measures how grant writers spend their computer time. The closest sources measure other groups. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics counts writers and authors as one group, so its pay and job figures do not single out grant writers. The numbers below come from office workers and researchers. Read them with that gap in mind.

The first figure is from a 2018 Adobe survey of more than 1,000 office workers who own a smartphone. It measures time with personal email, not work email. The second is from the 2018 Federal Demonstration Partnership faculty workload survey. It found that principal investigators reported putting 44.3% of their time on federally funded projects into administrative tasks. That figure reached us through a 2023 SRA International blog, not the original report. The 2012 baseline differs between sources, so the change over time is uncertain.

Put those together and the pattern is clear enough. Administrative work takes a large share of research time, and email takes a real slice of the day. Your own split will differ. Track a normal week of work before you decide where a voice tool fits.
Working inside Grants.gov on a Mac

Grants.gov is the portal for federal applications. The applicant workflow runs in a fixed order. You find the opportunity, click Apply, and create a workspace. Then you add participants, complete the forms, and run Check Application. The last step is either Complete and Notify AOR or Sign and Submit. Each application gets its own workspace, so every deadline needs its own.

Accounts come first. Anyone who downloads forms or works on them online needs a Login.gov account. You also register on Grants.gov with a UEI from SAM.gov. Set up both early. A missing account can block a co-writer on the day before a deadline.
What autosave does and does not protect

Online forms are completed in the browser, inside the workspace. The system autosaves every five minutes. Autosave protects you from a crash or a closed tab. It does not protect you from a bad edit. If you paste the wrong budget figure into a field, autosave saves that mistake too. Keep a dated copy of each major version in your project folder.
Offline forms need Adobe Reader

Some forms can be completed offline as PDFs. Those need the free Adobe Reader installed on your Mac. Install it now, not on deadline afternoon. Open a test form in Adobe Reader before you rely on it. The Grants.gov applicant guide does not name a supported browser for the online workspace, so check the portal's own help before you start.
Where Lazur helps in the portal, and where it stops

Lazur sees your screen while you hold the shortcut. That helps on a dense form. Ask where a field is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to attach a file, and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click. Your hands stay on the mouse, and you make every change.

It stops at the submit step. Lazur does not click buttons, edit files, or operate other apps. When you reach Sign and Submit, ask Lazur to circle it. Then read the check results yourself and click the button yourself. Applying is your act, so that click stays with you.
Drafting narrative sections in Word and Google Docs

Most narrative sections start in Word or Google Docs. Lazur helps in both. In Word, it can point at a menu item, explain a style, or dictate text at the cursor. In Google Docs, it works in your browser, so the same voice help applies. For setup details, read [Word for grant writers](/for/grant-writers/word) and [Google Docs for grant writers](/for/grant-writers/google-docs).

Keep Word current. Microsoft's release notes say macOS 14 Sonoma is the minimum for receiving Microsoft 365 and Office updates. Check your macOS version with Apple menu > About This Mac. If your Mac is on an older release, update macOS before you plan a workflow around a newer feature.
Dictation for grant writers without losing your place

Hold fn and speak. Lazur types clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. This suits first drafts of the needs statement, the project summary, and the evaluation plan. Dictation is unlimited on the Pro and Power plans, so a long drafting session does not hit a cap.

Dictated text still needs a second pass. Speech tools miss funder names, program acronyms, and place names. Add those words to your personal dictionary before you start. Then read the draft aloud once. Your ear catches rhythm problems that your eyes skip.
Using AI for grant proposals within funder rules

Ask Lazur to explain a funder term you do not understand. Keep the guidelines on screen, hold ⌥ ⌘, and ask what the funder means by a phrase. Lazur answers out loud from what it sees. Then check the answer against the notice itself. A voice answer is a starting point, not the rule.

Some funders publish their own rules on AI use in applications. Read those rules before you use any AI draft. Your organization may have a policy too. Ask before you assume either way, and note who approved the approach.
Budgets, spreadsheets and the numbers reviewers check

Budgets are where small errors do the most damage. A total that does not match the budget justification can stall a review. Lazur can help you read the sheet. Hold ⌥ ⌘ on a total row and ask what the formula does. Lazur explains it out loud. In Excel, ask Lazur to point at the cells that feed a total, then trace the chain yourself with Formulas > Formula Auditing > Trace Precedents.

Budgets move between tools. If yours lives in Numbers, read [how to export Numbers to Excel on Mac](/how-to/export-a-spreadsheet-to-excel-in-numbers). If a funder wants a file from Google Sheets, read [how to download Google Sheets as Excel on Mac](/how-to/download-as-excel-in-google-sheets). Check the converted file before you send it, because formulas and formats can change. For more Excel help, see [Lazur for Excel](/apps/excel).

The costliest budget mistake is a stale total. Someone changes one line, the justification keeps the old figure, and nobody reads both side by side. Before you send, ask Lazur to read the justification aloud. Then compare it with the budget yourself. Lazur only sees what is on screen, so a figure on a hidden tab can slip past it.
Email with funders, partners and reviewers

Email takes real time in grant work. Reviewers and program staff ask follow-up questions. Partners send budget letters and commitment forms. The Adobe figure measures personal email, so it does not give your work email hours. It does show how much of a day one inbox can take.

Lazur helps with email in [Gmail](/apps/gmail). Ask it to draft a reply by voice, and it can point at the send button. If a message went out too early, use the steps in [how to undo send in Gmail on Mac](/how-to/undo-send-in-gmail). If your organization uses Outlook for Mac, check the build number. Microsoft's release notes list Outlook for Mac 16.114 and recent changes such as Data Loss Prevention.
Keeping funder and personnel data private

Grant work includes material you may not share. That can mean salary tables, participant records, unpublished financial statements, or a funder's review notes. Your organization sets the rules for that data, and you follow them. Lazur does not change those rules. It makes no compliance claim for your organization, and neither does this page.

Here is what happens to what Lazur sees. It listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers so Lazur can answer. They are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Lazur also keeps a memory of what you asked and did, on your Mac.

Before you ask a question, close windows that hold data you should not send to an outside service. Ask your IT or compliance contact whether AI assistants are allowed on the Mac that holds that data. If the answer is no, do that part of the work without the assistant.
A worked example from funder page to first draft

Take a funder notice for a community literacy program. Open the notice in your browser. Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask Lazur for the deadline and the page limit. Verify both against the PDF. Then ask Lazur to research recent awards from the same funder. The research runs in Lazur's own Chrome tabs through the Lazur for Chrome extension, and it returns a summary and a report.

Next, open your Word draft. Hold fn and dictate the needs statement in one pass. Ask Lazur to explain any funder term that feels unclear. Ask it to point at each section heading, so you see the structure at a glance. When the draft is done, check the page limit and the required headings against the notice. Save a dated copy.

Finally, open the Grants.gov workspace. Ask Lazur where Check Application lives, and run the check yourself. Read every error it reports. When the check passes, ask Lazur to circle Sign and Submit. Then click it yourself. The final click stays with you.
Edge cases that catch busy grant writers

Deadlines that fall close together need separate plans. Give each application its own folder, its own Grants.gov workspace, and its own Calendar events. Ask Lazur to add the internal review date and the funder deadline as separate events. Name them clearly, so they never swap.

Revisions after funder feedback are another trap. Turn on Track Changes in Word from Review > Track Changes, so reviewers see what moved. Ask Lazur to explain how to accept or reject a single change. Then accept only the changes you checked. A bulk accept can hide an edit you did not mean to keep.
Mistakes grant writers make with AI tools

items: Trusting a spoken answer about a deadline without opening the notice itself.
Dictating while the wrong window is active, so the text lands in a budget cell or an email.
Forgetting that anyone who works on the forms online needs a Login.gov account.
Leaving protected personnel or participant records on screen while Lazur is listening.
Letting autosave hide a bad edit instead of keeping dated copies of each version.
Sending an AI draft without checking the funder's rules on AI use.

blocks.text: Lazur answers out loud, so anyone near you can hear the answer. Use headphones in a shared office. A quiet room also helps dictation, because background speech can end up in your draft.
Where to start

Start with one task. Pick the work that repeats most often, such as reading funder notices or checking a budget justification. Use Lazur for that task for a full week. Then decide whether it earns a place in your routine. The Pro trial needs no credit card and starts when you first open the app. Current plans are on [the pricing page](/pricing), and the Mac app is on [the download page](/download).

If your work also covers research, see [Lazur for researchers](/for/researchers). That page covers grants, email and Word in more detail. If your work leans on drafting, see [Lazur for writers](/for/writers) for dictation across Pages, Word and Google Docs.
Not sure how your speaking pace compares with your typing? Try the [speaking vs typing test](/tools/speaking-vs-typing-test) before you decide how much to dictate.

faq.question: Can an AI assistant write my grant proposal for me?
faq.answer: Lazur drafts and types text when you ask, and it dictates your words at the cursor. It does not write a proposal on its own. You read every line, check it against the funder's notice, and decide what goes in.

faq.question: Does Lazur submit applications on Grants.gov?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons or operate other apps. It can point at Sign and Submit and explain what the button does. You click it yourself.

faq.question: Does Lazur watch my screen all the time?
faq.answer: No. It listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers so Lazur can answer, and they are not stored.

faq.question: Can I use Lazur with confidential grant or personnel data?
faq.answer: Follow your organization's rules for that data first. Lazur does not make compliance claims for you, and it does not replace your IT or compliance team. If your rules forbid AI tools on that data, keep the assistant closed.

faq.question: Does Lazur work inside Word and Google Docs?
faq.answer: Lazur sees your screen in any app while you hold the shortcut. It is not a plugin or add-in for Word or Google Docs. Read Lazur for Word and Lazur for Google Docs to see what it can point at in each.

faq.question: Does Lazur run on Windows?
faq.answer: Not yet. Lazur is a Mac app for Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, but it is not available.

faq.question: How does Lazur research funders?
faq.answer: Research runs in Lazur's own Chrome tabs with the Lazur for Chrome extension. It comes back with a summary and a report. Check each funder's site terms before you run research there, and verify results against the source.

faq.question: Does Lazur replace a grant consultant or development officer?
faq.answer: No. It helps you read notices, find fields, draft and dictate text, and hear answers out loud. Strategy, funder relationships, and final judgment stay with people.

painPoints.title: Portal steps that hide the next click
painPoints.text: Grants.gov work happens in a browser workspace with a fixed workflow. Finding the right field or step can eat an afternoon when the deadline is close.

painPoints.title: Funder rules buried in long PDFs
painPoints.text: Page limits, required headings, and font rules sit inside long notices. Checking each one by hand is slow, and one missed rule can sink a draft.

painPoints.title: Budgets that drift out of sync
painPoints.text: A line changes in the budget, but the justification keeps the old figure. Reviewers notice the mismatch, and fixing it late costs time you do not have.

painPoints.title: Email that never stops
painPoints.text: Program staff, partners, and reviewers send follow-up questions all week. Replies pile up while the draft waits in a separate window.

painPoints.title: A slow first draft
painPoints.text: A needs statement or project summary takes longer when you type every word. Some writers find speaking gets the first version down faster.

painPoints.title: Problems that show up on deadline day
painPoints.text: A missing account or an unread error can surface on the last afternoon, when there is no time left to fix it.
